_note: Fictional study templates. Slots {units},{unit},{treatment},{outcome},{confounder},{running},{cutoff},{n} are filled from topics. Every answer is fixed by the template (no LLM).

topics.confounder: the severity of a prior economic crisis

topics.running: vote share in the last election

fields.unit: What is the unit of observation?
fields.assumption: What is the key identifying assumption?
fields.estimand: What does the main comparison estimate?
fields.threat: What is the main weakness or threat to validity?
fields.adjusts: What does this design adjust for?

templates.text: Researchers randomly assigned half of {n} {units} to receive {treatment}; the other half received nothing. A year later they compared average {outcome} between the two groups.
templates.assumption: Random assignment makes the two groups identical on average in all pretreatment characteristics, observed and unobserved.
templates.estimand: The sample average treatment effect (SATE), via the difference in means.
templates.threat: External validity: the units studied may not represent the population or setting we care about.
templates.adjusts: All pretreatment characteristics, observed and unobserved, on average (through randomization).

templates.text: A government used a public lottery to decide which of {n} {units} would receive {treatment}. Researchers later compared average {outcome} between lottery winners and losers.
templates.assumption: The lottery assigned treatment as if at random, so winners and losers are comparable on average.
templates.estimand: The average effect of the treatment among the units in the lottery.
templates.threat: The as-if-random assumption could fail (e.g., the lottery was manipulated); check balance on pretreatment variables.
templates.adjusts: Pretreatment differences between groups, to the extent assignment was truly as-if random.

templates.text: Researchers compared this year's {outcome} in {units} that chose to adopt {treatment} with {units} that did not.
templates.assumption: Adopters and non-adopters are comparable on everything related to the outcome except the treatment.
templates.estimand: The difference in average outcomes between adopters and non-adopters after treatment.
templates.threat: Confounding / selection bias: units self-selected into treatment and may differ, e.g., in {confounder}.
templates.adjusts: Nothing beyond the comparison itself; it relies on the groups being comparable.

templates.text: Worried that {units} adopting {treatment} differ in {confounder}, researchers compared {outcome} between adopters and non-adopters only within groups of {units} with the same level of {confounder}.
templates.assumption: Within each subclass, adopters and non-adopters are comparable apart from the treatment.
templates.estimand: The treatment-control difference within subclasses defined by a confounder.
templates.threat: Unobserved confounders can still bias the estimate; only the subclassified variable is controlled.
templates.adjusts: The observed confounder used to form the subclasses ({confounder}).

templates.text: Researchers measured {outcome} in {units} the year before they adopted {treatment} and again the year after, and compared the two years.
templates.assumption: No time trend: absent treatment, the outcome would not have changed between the two periods.
templates.estimand: The change in the treated units' average outcome from before to after.
templates.threat: Time-varying confounders: a general trend could produce the change without the treatment.
templates.adjusts: Unit-specific confounders that do not change over time.

templates.text: Researchers measured {outcome} before and after some {units} adopted {treatment}, in both the adopting {units} and a set of {units} that never adopted it. They compared the change in adopters with the change in non-adopters.
templates.assumption: Parallel trends: without treatment, the adopters' outcome would have followed the same time trend as the non-adopters'.
templates.estimand: The sample average treatment effect for the treated (SATT).
templates.threat: Non-parallel trends: if adopters were already on a different trajectory, the estimate is biased.
templates.adjusts: Time-invariant unit differences and time trends shared by both groups.

templates.text: {Units} qualified for {treatment} only if their {running} exceeded {cutoff}. Researchers compared {outcome} for {units} just above and just below {cutoff}.
templates.assumption: Nothing else changes discontinuously at the threshold, so the jump in outcome is due to the treatment alone.
templates.estimand: The average treatment effect for units near the threshold.
templates.threat: External validity: the effect may not generalize to units far from the threshold.
templates.adjusts: Confounding, by comparing units that are nearly identical except for crossing the threshold.

templates.text: In an RD study of {treatment} with a threshold at {cutoff} of {running}, researchers re-ran the analysis using {outcome} measured in the year BEFORE the program existed as the outcome.
templates.design: Placebo test (of a regression discontinuity design)
templates.assumption: The treatment cannot affect an outcome measured before it existed, so the true effect is zero.
templates.estimand: An effect that should be approximately zero if the RD design is valid.
templates.threat: A large placebo 'effect' would signal sorting or manipulation around the threshold.
templates.adjusts: It does not estimate an effect; it checks the design's validity.

templates.text: Researchers obtained a complete list of all {units} and randomly drew {n} of them without replacement, each with equal chance, to measure {outcome}.
templates.assumption: Every unit on the sampling frame has an equal, known chance of selection, so the sample is representative on average.
templates.estimand: The population average {outcome}, estimated by the sample average.
templates.threat: Nonresponse or an incomplete sampling frame can still introduce bias.
templates.adjusts: Sample selection bias, for observed and unobserved characteristics.

templates.text: Interviewers approached {units} until the sample's mix of {confounder} matched census figures, then measured {outcome}.
templates.assumption: Matching on the quota variables makes the sample representative on everything else too.
templates.estimand: The population average {outcome}, estimated from a quota sample.
templates.threat: Sample selection bias on unobserved characteristics (interviewers choose whom to approach).

templates.text: With no national list of {units}, researchers randomly selected regions, then randomly selected {units} within the chosen regions, and measured {outcome}.
templates.assumption: Random selection at every stage gives each unit a known probability of selection.
templates.threat: Selection probabilities are only approximately known in practice; nonresponse can bias results.
templates.adjusts: The lack of a complete sampling frame and the cost of reaching distant units.

templates.text: To measure a sensitive attitude, researchers randomly split respondents: one group was read a list of 3 items, the other the same list plus a sensitive item. Respondents reported only HOW MANY items they supported.
templates.assumption: The two randomized groups are comparable, and adding the sensitive item does not change answers to the other items.
templates.estimand: The proportion supporting the sensitive item: the difference in mean item counts.
templates.threat: Floor and ceiling effects: answering 0 or the maximum reveals the respondent's true answer.
templates.adjusts: Social desirability bias, by giving respondents anonymity through aggregation.

templates.text: In an experiment on {treatment}, one arm of randomly assigned {units} received only a notice saying they were being studied, with no other intervention. Researchers compared its {outcome} with the control group's.
templates.design: A randomized treatment arm isolating the Hawthorne effect
templates.assumption: Random assignment makes the arms comparable, so the difference reflects only the effect of being observed.
templates.estimand: The effect of knowing one is being observed (the Hawthorne effect).
templates.threat: Subjects may behave differently simply because they know they are observed.
templates.adjusts: It separates the effect of being observed from the effect of the substantive treatment.

templates.text: Officials identified the {units} with the worst {outcome} last year and gave them {treatment}. This year those {units} improved substantially, and officials credited the program.
templates.design: A before-and-after comparison of units selected for extreme values
templates.assumption: The improvement would not have happened without the program.
templates.estimand: The change in the selected units' outcome.
templates.threat: Regression towards the mean: units selected for extreme values tend to move toward the average by chance alone.
templates.adjusts: Nothing; the selection on extreme outcomes makes chance improvement likely.
